Intel pointed to a few risks for the second half of the year. answer: The call didn't cover Bitcoin or crypto mining. Nobody at NVIDIA, and none of the analysts asking questions, brought it up. The demand they talked about came from artificial intelligence: big cloud companies, AI labs, smaller cloud providers (which NVIDIA calls "NeoClouds"), businesses, and governments building their own AI computing.

On the call, Intel's finance chief named a few risks for the second half of 2026. The biggest one: rising input costs (what Intel pays for the parts and materials it needs), especially memory chips. He called these "growing headwinds", meaning forces that make it harder to make money. He also said Intel 18A, its newest manufacturing process, is still early in its ramp (the phase when a new factory process is slowly scaled up to full production). Early on, that tends to be costly. Both of these work against gross margin, which is the share of each sales dollar left after paying to make the product. He also said the factories would add supply in the third and fourth quarters at a slower pace than Intel expected three months earlier.

answer: Yes. Ford raised its full-year forecast for adjusted EBIT, now expecting $8.5 billion to $10.5 billion. (EBIT is profit from running the business before interest and taxes; "adjusted" means one-off items are stripped out; "guidance" is the company's own forecast.) Most of the raise came from Ford Blue, its gas and hybrid vehicle unit, whose forecast went up by $500 million. Forecasts for its other units stayed the same. Ford also kept its free cash flow forecast at $5 billion to $6 billion. Free cash flow is the cash left after paying for operations and investments. Ford's first quarter beat expectations, but the CFO said part of that came from costs landing earlier or later than planned, so Ford chose not to count that toward the raise.
